characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: D/MAX-2500/PC with Cu Kα X-ray tube (ASTM: D5380-93[2014])
characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.0Be shows austenite γ + ferrite δ together with Be11Fe (orange (011) peak near 49°, peak near 86°) and Be2Fe (green-star peak near 72°); precipitate peaks grow with Be content.

characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.0Be shows a wavy, banded two-phase structure: lighter bands labelled α-Fe, dark particle-decorated bands labelled Be–Fe phase, matrix γ-Fe, and annealing twins.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: RD–ND plane; standard metallographic preparation (#400–#5000 sandpapers then 0.5 µm diamond polishing); etched with 8% nitrate alcohol solution; surface finish 0.05 µm

characterization_methods.key_findings: 1.0Be phase map: green austenite with scattered red ferrite patches along boundaries and in bands; mixed low- and high-angle boundaries; broader, more uniform KAM green/yellow distribution; average grain size ≈11 µm.

characterization_methods.purpose: study grain structure, phase distribution, grain-boundary character and KAM

characterization_methods.key_findings: 1.0Be matrix is primarily austenite (SADP); Be2C precipitates present (coarse particles; [011] zone axis), with Be2C size increasing with Be content; dislocations appear as straight planar bands with localised clusters (Fig. 15, Fig. 16b).
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Samples thinned to 40 µm with waterproof sandpaper then dual-jet electrochemical polishing in 10% perchloric acid + 90% ethanol at 26.5 V and −20 °C
characterization_methods.purpose: observe matrix, precipitates and dislocations of the rolled 1.0Be steel

characterization_methods.key_findings: The 1.0Be fracture shows dimples mixed with flatter, quasi-cleavage-like facets and shallow platforms; the dissociation/cleavage surface gradually increases from 0.5Be to 1.5Be.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: tensile fracture surface of the rolled 1.0Be specimen (50 µm scale bar, Fig. 12c)

characterization_methods.key_findings: The 1.0Be DSC peak is at 1163.3 °C; Be addition shifts the transformation peak of the alloy from a high-temperature event near 1320 °C (0Be) to ~1155–1166 °C, and the 1.0Be point decreased only slightly relative to 0.5Be.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: heating rate 10 °C/min; heating curves after homogenisation
characterization_methods.purpose: determine the phase transformation temperature as a function of Be content

characterization_methods.key_findings: Rolled 1.0Be: matrix (austenite) 398.39 ±14.630 HV and ferrite 349.81 ±21.267 HV.

characterization_methods.purpose: measure the microhardness of the matrix and ferrite in the rolled 1.0Be steel

computational_details.simulation_method: thermodynamic / CALPHAD equilibrium calculation of the Fe–Be binary phase diagram
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Consistent with the observed Be–Fe phase distribution: austenite can dissolve <1% Be while ferrite dissolves much more, and excess Be precipitates as compounds.

analytical_models.equation_role: compute sample volume and density from buoyancy measurements
analytical_models.model_note: V0 = (m1 − m2)/ρ_water (Eq. 1) and ρ0 = m0/V0 (Eq. 2), where m0 is the mass of the experimental steel; used for the rolled 1.0Be density value.

analytical_models.equation_role: determine whether an infinite solid solution can form
analytical_models.model_note: Δr = |(rA − rB)/rA| (Eq. 3); when radius difference <8% and crystal structure matches, an infinite solid solution can form. Be does not form an infinite solid solution in the iron matrix.

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: Stress concentration is evident at the precipitation locations of the carbide and the Be–Fe phase, and the distribution of these precipitates is primarily concentrated at the grain boundary and phase interface; dislocation density increases with Be content (KAM hot-spots decorate boundaries).

interfaces.interface_notes: The rolled 1.0Be steel is a banded dual-phase γ + α/δ structure with annealing twins; Be–Fe phase particles are dispersed along the rolling direction.
interfaces.phase_evolution: The as-cast needle-like (ancient Chinese character shaped) Be–Fe phase transforms after hot rolling into spherical and point-like shapes; needle-like compounds decrease and punctate compounds increase, and the distribution changes from aggregate to dispersed, mostly on the austenite matrix.
interfaces.slip_behavior: Under external force a large number of dislocation slip movements and accumulation occur inside the steel (b0048); for 1.0Be quasi-dissociation cracks initially occur and rapidly expand inside brittle ferrite grains and are hindered at the adjacent austenite (b0069).

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: density (while maintaining a high strength–ductility product)
comparative_performance.improvement_percentage: -21.38% (Be steel density lower than pure iron)

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloys were made of high-purity elements Fe, Mn, Al, C and Be (each 99.99%) and melted into alloy ingots in a vacuum induction melting furnace under high-purity argon. Ingot diameter 60 mm, thickness 30 mm. This as-cast ingot is the precursor (proc_as-cast) of the rolled 1.0Be strip.
17 times hot rolling with two-high mill rolls at 1050°C (1.5 mm per roll, strain rate of 0.6 s^-1), producing a 5 mm plate.
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: 83% total deformation (17 passes, 1.5 mm per pass, final plate thickness 5 mm)

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: After each rolling pass the sample was kept in a muffle furnace for 3 min to maintain the rolling temperature.
After the last pass of rolling, water cooling was performed until cooled to room temperature.

structures.number_of_phases: 2 (austenite γ + ferrite α/δ; plus Be–Fe and Be2C precipitates)
structures.overall_structure: Rolled 1.0Be steel exhibits a wavy, banded dual-phase structure of austenite (γ) + ferrite (α/δ) with dispersed Be–Fe phase (Be11Fe, Be2Fe) particles and Be2C carbide precipitates; annealing twins are present. With increasing Be content the single γ structure converts into a banded α + γ dual-phase structure with dispersed Be–Fe phase.

unmapped_findings: Atomic sizes of the elements in the steels (Table 5 / Fig. 18): Fe 124 pm, Mn 124 pm, Al 143 pm, Be 111 pm, C 77 pm; Mn, Al and Be form substitution solid solutions while C forms an interstitial solid solution.

Lattice-distortion behaviour relevant to the 1.0Be steel: the Be atom (111 pm) is smaller than Fe (124 pm) so it causes inward lattice shrinkage, whereas Al (143 pm) causes outward lattice expansion; although Be density is low (1.87 g/cm³), its inward lattice distortion means Be does not have a strong lightweighting effect on the density.

Per the Fe–Be binary phase diagram, essentially no Be is soluble in austenite (Be solubility in austenite <1%) and Be precipitates as compounds once the austenite is saturated, whereas ferrite can dissolve much larger amounts of Be; this explains the Be–Fe phase distribution (the 1.0Be rolled steel dissolves more Be in the ferrite, reducing precipitate content relative to 1.5Be).

After hot deformation the as-cast needle-like (ancient Chinese character shaped) Be–Fe phase in the 1.0Be steel is transformed into spherical and point shapes, most Be being solubilised into the matrix, which reduces the precipitate content.

DSC of the 1.0Be alloy shows a phase transformation peak at 1163.3 °C (after homogenisation, heating at 10 °C/min); Be addition shifts the transformation temperature of the alloy down by roughly 120 °C relative to the Be-free steel.
